mt_stone_hill_2.blurb: Stone Hill lies in the Kootenai National Forest of northwest Montana, close to Lake Koocanusa and the town of Eureka, among open ponderosa pines with views over the water. Roped climbing is split almost evenly between bolted sport lines and trad, with a smaller helping of boulder problems. The bulk of the roped routes sit between 5.10 and 5.11, yet there are plenty of 5.7 to 5.9 climbs for newer leaders and a handful pushing into 5.13. The stone is a very hard quartzite: sharp edges, thin cracks, slabs and small roofs. The Eastside and Westside of the Reservoir hold most of the climbs. Climbing runs from about late February to late October.

ut_potash_road.blurb: Potash Road follows the Colorado River just outside Moab, where sandstone walls rise steeply from a narrow river gorge. Many crags sit right beside the pavement, so the walk-in is short or nonexistent. Trad is the main event, with a solid supply of sport routes and a few boulders and aid lines. Grades run from easy slabs to 5.12 and a little beyond, though most routes land between 5.10 and 5.12, with a modest number of 5.8 and 5.9 climbs. The rock offers flakes, slabs, nubbins and edges. Wall Street is the biggest wall, while Long Canyon and Day Canyon branch off with more routes; Day Canyon has separate shady and sunny sections.

mn_duluth_bouldering.blurb: Duluth sits on the western tip of Lake Superior, and its boulders are woven into the city itself, some of them next to ordinary roads, while others lie along forested trails and streams. Bouldering is nearly everything here, with only a scattering of sport, trad and top-rope lines. Problems run from very easy up to the V10 range, but the bulk fall between V0 and V4, so there is a lot for newer boulderers. The local outcrops vary in stone, from gabbro to granite. Little Foxx Canyon is the largest cluster, followed by the Spirit Mountain boulders and the boulders in Brewer's Park, a city park in West Duluth.

nm_diablo_canyon.blurb: Diablo Canyon is a dry canyon in the Santa Fe area that cuts between tall cracked basalt cliffs toward the Rio Grande. Sport climbing leads by a wide margin, with a smaller number of trad lines, and some walls hold multi-pitch routes. Most climbs fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a good number of 5.13s and a couple of routes touching 5.14; easier climbs exist but are limited. The basalt gives solid holds, though less-travelled lines can have loose sections. The Grotto, the Shack and Eden Canyon hold the most routes. Spring and fall are the most comfortable seasons, winter mornings are cold but workable, and summer gets very hot with little shade in much of the canyon.

va_blue_ridge_parkway.blurb: This stretch of the Blue Ridge Parkway near Charlottesville is mainly a bouldering destination, with a smaller amount of older trad and top-rope climbing on cliffs up to about 200 feet. Most boulder problems run from V0 to V6, with enough harder ones to reach double-digit grades; the roped climbs mostly sit between 5.7 and 5.10. The stone is largely greenstone, which has sharp edges and can feel soft and flaky in places yet solid in others, plus some bands of granite. The Forest is the biggest boulder zone and runs noticeably cooler than Charlottesville, while Love Gap holds the main cliff. Climbing is possible through the year.

ca_hwy_33_ojai.blurb: Highway 33 climbs north from Ojai into the Los Padres National Forest, and the climbing is strung along the road and the creeks beside it. Bouldering makes up most of the total, followed by sport routes and a smaller amount of trad. Boulder problems cover everything from easy to V10 and beyond, mostly V0 to V5, while roped climbs are mainly 5.8 to 5.11. Most of the stone is sandstone. Wheeler Gorge, a creek-side sport crag, mixes sandstone with conglomerate cobbles and green schist, and it is usable through the year because the creek corridor keeps it cool in summer. Some of the sandstone boulders sit in shaded riverbeds, which suit the warmer months.
